stimulus.text:
A historian argues: 'The arrival of enslaved Africans in Virginia in 1619 established race-based slavery in the British colonies, and the plantation slavery of the mid-1700s was essentially the same system that began in 1619.' Virginia's laws on slavery hardened step by step:

| Year | Law or case | What it did |
| 1640 | John Punch | A Black runaway and two white runaways were caught together; the white men got four more years added to their terms, while Punch was condemned to slavery for life. |
| 1655 | John Casor | A Northampton County court declared Casor, an African servant, a slave for life — the first civil-court ruling of its kind in the English colonies. |
| 1662 | Partus sequitur ventrem | A child's status followed the mother, so the children of enslaved women were born enslaved — breaking English common law, where status followed the father. |
| 1667 | Baptism | Virginia declared that baptism did not free an enslaved person. |
| 1705 | Slave code | Virginia gathered its slave laws into one code: 'All Negro, mulatto and Indian slaves within this dominion… shall be held to be real estate.' |
stimulus.source_note: Original table written for this question from Barron's 2027 Ch 4, 5 Steps 2024 Ch 8, and the Virginia slave code of 1705 (public domain). The Casor date follows the March 8, 1655 Northampton County ruling; Barron's dates the Casor case to 1640, which conflates it with the John Punch case of 1640.

source: original; stimulus is an original secondary passage written for this question

books.section: The Nature of Slavery in British North America

primary_sources: Johnson v. Parker, Northampton County court ruling (March 8, 1655)

stem: Which of the following most weakens the historian's claim?

options.text: In the 1660s Virginia made enslaved status pass from mother to child and denied freedom to the baptized, so the system took shape decades after 1619.
Because English planters wanted African labor from the start, the change from indentured servants to enslaved Africans in the Chesapeake was complete within a year of the 1619 arrival.
options.misconception: The change took decades of lawmaking; the 1619 arrival did not create a complete system.

options.text: The profitable tobacco economy was the single cause of slavery's growth, so Virginia's slave system would have looked the same in 1754 even without the laws passed in the 1660s.
options.misconception: A single cause cannot carry the story; the laws created hereditary racial slavery.

options.text: Africans in Virginia were enslaved on exactly the same legal terms and faced identical legal conditions as Africans in Barbados, since both colonies lived under the same English law.
options.misconception: Virginia built its own code from its own laws; Barbados was a template, not a copy.

rationales.general:
1. Read the historian's claim. Slavery arrived finished in 1619 and stayed the same until the mid-1700s.
2. Test it against the table. In 1640 a runaway got lifetime slavery while his white partners got four more years.
3. Test it again. In 1662 status followed the mother; in 1667 baptism stopped freeing anyone.
4. Name what the table shows. A system built law by law over decades — not one delivered in 1619.
Remember: a claim about 'always' falls to one dated change — find the first law that made it different.
rationales.A: The historian's claim says the system arrived finished in 1619 and stayed the same. The table shows otherwise: in the 1660s Virginia passed laws making enslaved status pass from mother to child and denying freedom to the baptized — new legal machinery that created hereditary, race-based bondage. That was a real change, not a continuation of 1619. The plantation slavery of the mid-1700s was a system built law by law over decades. The other options defend the claim instead of weakening it, or rest on a single cause.
rationales.B: The change took decades of lawmaking; the 1619 arrival did not create a complete system.
rationales.C: A single cause cannot carry the story; the laws created hereditary racial slavery.
rationales.D: Background: Virginia built its own code from its own laws; Barbados was a template, not a copy.
